title: The U.S. electorate is more ideologically heterodox than party labels suggest, with family autonomy, economic intervention and international role cutting across coalitions
source_unit: Searchlight Institute, How to Build a Supermajority; Searchlight Policy Values Surveys 1 and 2
geography: United States; adults weighted to the November 2024 electorate

observations.period: June 5–July 7, 2026; U.S. adults weighted to 2024 electorate

denominator.unit: U.S. adults recruited online by RepData; weighted to the 2024 electorate

consistent_conservatism.unit: percent classified as completely ideologically conservative

consistent_liberalism.unit: percent classified as completely ideologically liberal

heterodox_majority.value: The large remainder holds combinations of liberal, conservative and cross-pressured views that are not captured by a single left-right scale

policy_axes.value: Five axes structure the analysis: gender and gender roles, America’s international role, parental authority and family, the economic role of government, and order versus openness

observations.method: Searchlight Policy Values Survey 1: 5,807 U.S. adults recruited online, with an oversample of unregistered respondents and raking to the 2024 electorate on demographic and vote variables; effective sample size 5,021.
observations.uncertainty: The segmentation is model-dependent and sponsored by the Searchlight Institute; online recruitment, screening, weighting and the choice of axes shape the resulting groups and do not prove stable causal coalitions.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults eligible or potentially eligible for the electorate, with derived policy-value segments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Party identity still matters and may organize many responses; heterodox issue profiles do not guarantee cross-party voting or durable coalition behavior.

observations.period: 2026 policy-values analysis; family autonomy and economic role

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Searchlight Policy Values Survey 1

parental_autonomy_salience.value: Keeping government out of parental discipline except abuse or neglect produced a +9.1 percentage-point effect on hypothetical candidate choice

social_security_protection.value: A position to reduce Social Security benefits to keep taxes stable produced a −8.2 percentage-point effect on hypothetical candidate choice

rich_taxation.value: The position to keep taxes lower on high-income individuals produced a −4.4 percentage-point effect

consumer_autonomy.value: The report identifies broad support for government staying out of personal consumer choices alongside support for an active redistributive economic role

observations.method: Randomized hypothetical-candidate conjoint tasks embedded in Searchlight Survey 1; effects are reported as percentage-point changes in candidate choice relative to control positions.
observations.uncertainty: Hypothetical vote-choice effects depend on wording, issue set, control conditions and survey context; they are directional estimates, not election forecasts or observed policy outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Full weighted U.S. adult sample, with partisan and segment analyses in the source.
observations.counterinterpretation: High salience in a conjoint task does not mean voters prioritize the issue in a real election when candidates, events and campaign information interact.

observations.period: June–August 2026; international role and economic stability

denominator.unit: U.S. adults recruited online by RepData in Searchlight Policy Values Survey 2, weighted to the 2024 electorate

economic_stability_isolationism.value: Respondents reporting financial instability were 10 percentage points more likely to say the U.S. should focus on problems at home rather than global affairs

cross_party_home_focus.value: The home-focused international-role position appears among populist-leaning segments on both sides of the aisle

aid_position.value: In the conjoint experiment, maintaining current military aid to Israel had positive effects among Democrats (+8.9) and Republicans (+1.7) relative to the tested control
aid_position.unit: percentage-point impact in hypothetical candidate choice

china_position_salience.value: Standing up to China was characterized as a low-salience issue in the report’s testing

observations.method: Searchlight Policy Values Survey 2: 3,068 U.S. adults recruited online August 7–19, 2026, weighted to the 2024 electorate; effective sample size 2,452, plus topical and conjoint questions.
observations.uncertainty: The financial-stability relationship is associational and the international-role effects are based on hypothetical choices; neither establishes that economic hardship causes isolationism or predicts foreign-policy voting.
observations.subgroup: Respondents grouped by self-reported financial stability, party and derived policy segment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Economic instability may correlate with age, region, education, race, ideology or media exposure; the reported ten-point difference may not survive full adjustment or replicate outside this survey.

denominator.unit: derived policy-value groups identified from five analytical axes

cross_pressured_segments.value: The report identifies groups combining progressive economic views with traditional cultural views, or conservative economic views with support for humanitarian aid and public healthcare

trad_digital.value: A younger, online and ideologically diverse group split its 2024 vote almost equally while combining relatively progressive economics with traditional culture

pocketbook_center.value: The Center Square group is described as less likely to be registered, with few strong policy priorities and a strong pocketbook focus

coalition_implication.value: The report argues durable majorities require issue-specific heterodoxy rather than assuming a single ideological base has uniform preferences

observations.method: Derived segmentation from survey responses across the five value axes, combined with party, demographic, economic-stability and vote-reflection variables.
observations.uncertainty: Named segments are analytic constructions rather than official demographic groups; labels and boundaries depend on the model, selected questions and source organization’s strategic framing.
observations.subgroup: Nine derived U.S. electorate segments, including ideologically consistent and cross-pressured groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coalition profiles can help expose heterogeneity but can also overstate coherence within groups and understate campaign context, geographic variation and turnout differences.

related_sources.claim: Survey 1 toplines with field dates, sample, weighting, policy batteries and conjoint estimates.
Survey 2 toplines with August fieldwork, topical questions, predictors and second-wave weighting.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. political-values mechanism: party labels conceal cross-pressured coalitions, and economic stability, family autonomy, government role and international posture can recombine across partisan lines. It is a Searchlight Institute-sponsored survey and model-based segmentation with hypothetical conjoint experiments, not a neutral election forecast, probability-sample-only panel, observed voting behavior, causal public-opinion model or proof that the proposed supermajority coalition will form.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Searchlight article and two linked topline PDFs were retrieved and reviewed for field dates, sample, weighting, effective sample size, five axes, nine segments, conjoint effects, financial-stability/international-role association and issue-salience claims; both PDFs were hashed.
